sweep_summary: tari1263 (Tarifiyt / Rif Berber) is not in the catalog. Of the 16 title hits, only the McClelland records (1996 UT Arlington dissertation; 2000 Mellen book, two Glottolog duplicates) are about this language; the rest are Kabyle (Chaker x4, Mettouchi), Tashlhiyt (Gordon & Nafi, Boukous x2, Jebbour, Moktadir), Central Atlas Tamazight (Iazzi), or pan-Berber (Louali 2003, Brugnatelli 2005). No open copy of any McClelland work exists (Google Books no preview; not in UTA repositories; archive.org nothing), but the Google Books feed returned a verbatim snippet from McClelland 2000 p. 5 (§2.1.1): 'no phonemic word stress (C. McClelland 1985)' —. Louali 2003 (Köppe, pp. 67-77; her accent work is Siwi/Tuareg) and Brugnatelli 2005 (Quaderni di Semitistica 25) are print only. Newly downloaded and read: Vycichl & Chaker 1984 'Accent' (Encyclopédie berbère 1, OpenEdition), whose only Rif content is that Sarrionandia 1905 marks accent 'sans donner de règles précises'. The best first-hand placement statement actually read is Sarrionandia's §45 (already held by the project; page scan pp. 26-28 transcribed by eye because the archive.org scanned interleaves the columns): polysyllables are generally paroxytone (penultimate), some penult/antepenult variation, dialectal variation with r, shifts under affixation. Abdel-Massih 1971 §I.4 (final stress, non-contrastive) is for Ayt Seghrouchen, which Glottolog lumps into tari1263 but is not Rif. Acquisition priorities: McClelland 2000 (high; Mellen print) and McClelland 2008 A Phonology of Tarifit Berber (LINCOM, not in the item list, no preview) for a modern statement; McClelland 1996 and Louali 2003 medium.

new_statements.translation: we always mark the vowel on which the word's tonic accent falls, when the word has several vowels. About this accent we make the following remarks: 1. Polysyllabic words are generally paroxytone, i.e. they carry the accent on the penultimate syllable; e.g. man ár-gaç, woman zám-gharz, donkey ágh-iul, she-donkey zágh-iulz; take (you) ét-tef, take it étte-fiz, take them ette-fi-zen, take them (pl. addressee) ette-fét-ten. 2. In some polysyllabic words the accent falls on the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable; e.g. king áyellidh or ayéllidh [...] 3. In many words containing r the tonic accent varies according to the speech of the different localities.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is normally on the penultimate syllable of polysyllables; a minority of words fluctuate between penult and antepenult (the footnote explains these as trisyllables that speakers reduce to two syllables, making them penultimate too); words with r show locality-dependent placement (western vs eastern Rif); and stress moves when affixes are added so as to stay penultimate (ik-kár 'he says', ik-ká-rai 'he tells me', ik-ka-rá-sen 'he tells them', p. 26).
new_statements.exceptions: 2.ª: some polysyllables take penult or antepenult (áyellidh ~ ayéllidh, ámeçuar ~ améçuar, ziçûrin ~ ziçûurin, átenghedh ~ aténghedh, ánelmedh ~ anélmedh); 3.ª: words with r vary by locality (Ohran ~ Ohéran, zéyresz ~ zeyérsz, el Méghreb ~ el Meghéreb, tétteregh ~ tettéregh, etc; fn. 3: first pronunciation western Rif, second eastern kabilas); 4.ª (p. 28): 'el acento tónico de una palabra varía cuando ésta cambia de accidentes gramaticales, o se le añaden afijos o prefijos'. Contradicted for the Middle Atlas member of tari1263 by Abdel-Massih 1971 p. 17: 'Word stress in Tamazight is a non-contrastive feature. The occurence of word stress is predictable: primary stress falls on the last vowel of the word (i.e. /V/ or [ə]).'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms and inflected forms in a pedagogical grammar); auxiliary schwa vowels count as syllables only when stressed (§23, p. 11). No instrumental basis; modern Rif descriptions do not describe word stress, and Kossmann 2013 p. 7 says stress is non-phonemic 'if existent at all' in northern Berber west of Tunisia.
new_statements.identity_note: Two first-hand statements, for different varieties inside Glottolog's tari1263 and they disagree. (1) Sarrionandia (1905; 2nd ed. read) describes Rif Berber proper (Tarifit: Guelaia/Kelaia, Quebdana, Beni Snassen etc. as noted in his footnotes) and gives generally PENULTIMATE stress with local variation. (2) Abdel-Massih 1971 describes Middle Atlas 'Tamazight' with Ayt Ayache (Central Atlas Tamazight, cent2194 -- NOT tari1263) as the base dialect and Ayt Seghrouchen (Eastern Middle Atlas, lumped into tari1263 by Glottolog) in comparative notes; its stress rule (primary stress on the last vowel of the word, non-contrastive) is stated for 'Tamazight' generally and the Ayt Seghrouchen phonology notes (pp. 19-20) list no stress difference, so it applies to Ayt Seghrouchen only by default. Kossmann 2013 (p. 7) adds the general caveat that stress is non-phonemic 'if existent at all' in northern Berber west of Tunisia. The modern Tarifit descriptions (Kossmann 2000 Beni Iznasen; Mourigh & Kossmann 2020 Nador; Lafkioui 2007 atlas) have no stress section. If the catalog wants Tarifit proper, use Sarrionandia (old, missionary, impressionistic); if it accepts the Eastern Middle Atlas member, Abdel-Massih 1971 pp. 17-18 is a modern linguist's explicit rule (fixed: final syllable).

new_statements.translation: Regarding this accent we make the following remarks: 1. Polysyllabic words are generally paroxytone, i.e. they carry the accent on the penultimate syllable, e.g. man ár-gaç, woman zám-gharz, donkey ágh-iul, she-donkey zágh-iulz, take (you) ét-tef, take it ette-fiz, take them ette-fí-zen, take them (pl. imperative) ette-fét-ten. 2. In some polysyllables the accent falls on the penultimate or the antepenultimate, e.g. king áyellidh or ayéllidh, first ámeçuar or améçuar ... 3. In many words containing r the accent varies according to the speech of the different localities. 4. The accent of a word changes when it changes grammatical accidents or takes affixes or prefixes.
new_statements.citation: Sarrionandia, Pedro. Gramática de la lengua rifeña, 2.ª ed. (1st ed. Tánger: Imprenta Hispano-Arábiga, 1905). Cap. IV 'De la sílaba y del acento tónico', §45 'Del acento tónico'.
new_statements.reading: Sarrionandia (Rif, Tangier 1905) gives the only explicit placement rule found for Tarifit: default penultimate stress, with antepenultimate variants in some words, local variation, and shifts under affixation; a footnote (p. 27 n. 2) notes that apparent antepenultimate forms are pronounced as disyllables and so are 'also paroxytone'. Two later sources qualify it: Vycichl & Chaker 1984 (Encyclopédie berbère, 'Accent', par. 6, read) say he marks accent 'sans donner de règles précises', and McClelland 2000 (Mellen; Google Books snippet p. 5 only) states that Tarifit 'has no phonemic word stress (C. McClelland 1985)' — non-phonemic, which is compatible with a predictable penultimate default but is not itself a placement statement. Modern grammars held by the project (Mourigh & Kossmann 2020; Kossmann 2000; Lafkioui 2007, 2017) are silent on word stress; Kossmann 2013 (p. 7) calls stress non-phonemic 'if existent at all' in most northern Berber west of Tunisia. Abdel-Massih 1971 (final stress) is for Ayt Seghrouchen Tamazight, lumped under tari1263 by Glottolog but a different variety. Best coding for Rif proper, on present evidence: non-phonemic, penultimate default (Sarrionandia), weak.

[...] The rise occurs on the first vowel and thus coincides with the stressed syllable, with an F0 around 215 Hz [...] in Tarifit Berber, as in many other languages, focalisation is marked intonationally by an F0 rise accompanied by an increase in intensity.
